questions.stem: Which fundamental state of matter is characterised by having a definite volume, but no definite shape?
questions.explanation: Liquids have a definite volume because the particles are close together, but they lack a definite shape and will easily flow to take the shape of their container.

questions.stem: The physical process in which a solid changes directly into a gas without first passing through the liquid state is called:
questions.explanation: Sublimation is the direct transition from solid to gas. Common examples include dry ice (solid CO₂) and iodine crystals. The reverse process (gas to solid) is called deposition.

questions.explanation: Wait, the text got corrupted in the distractors. Clean version: Boyle's Law states that Pressure is inversely proportional to Volume when Temperature is constant (P ∝ 1/V, or PV = constant). If you squeeze a gas (increase pressure), its volume shrinks.

questions.stem: Charles's Law states that at a strictly constant pressure, the volume of a fixed mass of an ideal gas is directly proportional to its:
questions.explanation: Charles's Law states that V ∝ T (Volume is directly proportional to Absolute Temperature in Kelvin) when pressure is held constant. If you heat a gas, it expands.

questions.stem: In the Ideal Gas Equation (PV = nRT), what is the standard accepted value of the Universal Gas Constant (R) in SI units?
questions.explanation: In the International System of Units (SI), Pressure is in Pascals, Volume in m³, Temperature in Kelvin. The value of R is exactly 8.314 Joules per mole per Kelvin. 0.0821 is used when pressure is in atm and volume in litres.

questions.stem: Real gases strictly deviate from ideal behaviour under extreme conditions. Under what specific conditions do real gases behave MOST like an ideal gas?

options.option_text: At very high pressure and very low temperature.
At very high pressure and very high temperature.
At very low pressure and very low temperature.
At very low pressure and very high temperature.

questions.explanation: At high temperatures, gas molecules move fast enough to easily overcome intermolecular attractive forces. At low pressures, they are spread far apart, so their actual physical volume is negligible. Thus, under High T and Low P, real gases approximate ideal behaviour.
